questions.stem:
Using the source provided, respond to all parts of the question.

Your response to the question should be provided in six parts: A, B, C, D, E, and F. Write the response to each part of the question in complete sentences. Use appropriate psychological terminology in your response.

A. Identify the research method used in the study.

B. State the operational definition of cold pain tolerance.

C. Describe what the difference in the medians indicates for cold pain tolerance during the pre-medication phase and during the opioid medication infusion.

D. Identify one ethical guideline described in the study. Describe one way the researchers in the study applied this ethical guideline.

E. Explain the extent to which the research findings may or may not be generalizable using specific and relevant evidence from the study.

F. Explain how at least one of the research findings supports or refutes the placebo effect.
questions.context:
Introduction

In this study, researchers explored pain sensitivity and the effectiveness of opioid pain medication in people who are twins.

Participants

The study took place in the western United States. One hundred and nine pairs of twins (218 individual participants), including monozygotic and dizygotic twins,1 participated in the research. Participants were 18 to 70 years old and fluent in English, and they had received a negative pregnancy test result before participating. Demographic information about the twin pairs is included in the tables shown.

Table 1. Type of Twin Pair
Type of Twin Pair | Number of Pairs
Monozygotic (identical) | 78
Dizygotic (nonidentical) | 31

Table 2. Gender of Twin Pair
Gender | Monozygotic (identical) | Dizygotic (nonidentical)
Male twin pairs | 26 | 8
Female twin pairs | 50 | 12
Mixed-gender twin pairs | 0 | 13

Table 3. Race/Ethnicity of Twin Pair
Race/Ethnicity | Number of Twin Pairs
White | 58
Hispanic | 28
Asian | 15
African American | 5
American Indian | 2
Pacific Islander | 1

Before agreeing to participate in the study, individuals were given detailed information about the study’s purpose and procedures and were assured their involvement was voluntary. Individuals with underlying medical conditions, allergies to opioid medications, or a history of opioid addiction were excluded from the study. Trained laboratory staff were involved in the study to ensure the safety of the participants.

Method

Researchers conducted a single-session, double-blind, and placebo-controlled study that used a within-subjects design. Personal details were removed from all data collected from participants prior to storage in password-protected files, ensuring privacy and reducing the risk of unauthorized access.

The study consisted of a pre-medication phase of 140 minutes, followed by an infusion phase of 140 minutes.

During the pre-medication phase, participants’ blood samples were taken, their vital signs were checked, and their baseline sensitivity thresholds for heat pain and cold pain were established. Measurement of participants’ sensitivities included their thresholds for heat pain and cold pain and their tolerance for cold pain.

To assess heat pain, researchers placed a device on each participant’s forearm in contact with their skin. Starting at 35 degrees Celsius (~95° Fahrenheit), the temperature increased at a rate of 1°C/second (~1.8°F/second). Participants pushed a button to indicate when the temperature first felt painful. This procedure was repeated four times, and the average temperature that elicited pain was recorded as the “heat pain threshold.” The maximum temperature was limited to 52°C (~126°F) to prevent burn injuries.

To assess cold pain, researchers had participants immerse their hands in a container of ice water (temperature starting at 1–2°C/~34–35°F) with the palms of their hands in full contact with the bottom of the container. Participants indicated when they first started to feel pain and withdrew their hands once the pain became intolerable. The time when the pain sensation was first felt was recorded as the “cold pain threshold,” and the time when the participants withdrew their hands was recorded as the “cold pain tolerance.” The maximum duration was limited to 180 seconds (3 minutes) to prevent injuries.

During the infusion phase, one twin out of each pair was randomly assigned to receive an infusion of an opioid pain medication followed by an infusion of a saltwater-solution (a placebo). The other twin received the infusions in reverse order (saltwater-solution placebo followed by the opioid pain medication). The pain sensitivity tests for heat pain and cold pain were conducted during each condition.

Results and Discussion

During the pre-medication phase, the median cold pain threshold was 8.1 seconds, and the median cold pain tolerance was 16.2 seconds. The median heat pain threshold was 48.4°C (~119°F).

During the opioid medication infusion in the infusion phase, participants’ heat pain threshold increased by a median of 1.2°C (~2.2°F), meaning participants tolerated higher temperatures while taking the opioid medication. Participants’ cold pain threshold increased to a median of 14.3 seconds, and their cold pain tolerance increased to a median of 31.2 seconds. While taking the opioid medication, participants waited longer before reporting cold pain and tolerated the cold pain for a longer period.

The participants’ reported pain levels while taking the placebo were inconsistent—sometimes the pain levels were reported as increasing; other times the pain levels were reported as decreasing. Results of the comparisons between the opioid medication condition and the placebo condition are reported in Table 4.

Table 4. Median Pain Thresholds and Sensitivities Across All Twin Pairs
Pain Test | Pre-Medication Phase | During Saltwater Infusion (Placebo) | During Opioid Medication Infusion
Heat pain threshold | 48.4°C/119.12°F | 48.5°C/119.3°F | 49.6°C/121.3°F
Cold pain threshold | 8.1 seconds | 8.0 seconds | 14.3 seconds
Cold pain tolerance | 16.2 seconds | 15.6 seconds | 31.2 seconds

Because identical twins had more similar pain thresholds and pain tolerance responses than nonidentical twins, researchers found that pain threshold and pain tolerance were strongly linked to genetics.

Angst, M. S., Phillips, N. G., Drover, D. R., Tingle, M., Ray, A., Swan, G. E., Lazzeroni, L. C., & Clark, D. J. (2012). Pain, 153(7), 1397–1409.
questions.answer_text:
Sample responses from the source PDF. These are not official scoring guidelines.

A. The research method used in the study is a double‑blind, placebo‑controlled experiment employing a within‑subjects design. Each participant was exposed to both the opioid pain medication condition and the saltwater (placebo) condition, allowing comparison of pain thresholds and tolerance within the same individual across different treatment phases.

B. The operational definition of cold pain tolerance is the amount of time (measured in seconds) from when participants immersed their hands in ice water until they withdrew their hands because the cold pain became intolerable, with a maximum duration of 180 seconds to prevent injury.

C. The higher median during the opioid infusion shows that participants tolerated the cold pain for longer than they did in the pre-medication phase.

D. One ethical guideline was informed consent. The researchers applied this by giving participants detailed information about the study and making clear that participation was voluntary.

E. The findings are not fully generalizable. All participants were twins from the western United States and had to meet specific requirements, so the results may not apply to everyone.

F. The findings refute a strong placebo effect because the placebo results were inconsistent, while the opioid condition clearly increased cold pain tolerance.

questions.answer_text:
Sample responses from the source PDF. These are not official scoring guidelines.

A. Claim Being ghosted has negative impact on a person’s mental well-being because of (negative self-concept, low self-esteem, or increased anxiety)

B. Evidence and explanation from one source

According to Source 3, “after participants reflected on a ghosting experience, their anxiety increased from a mean of 1.61 to 1.90, and their low self-esteem increased from a mean of 1.84 to 2.24. The source states that these differences were statistically significant.”

This supports the claim because this can be explained through social rejection. Human beings have basic need to fit in, so being ignored or excluded can create distress. Because ghosting gives no clear reason for rejection, the person may feel uncertain, anxious, and less worthy.

C. Evidence from a different source and explanation using a different psychological concept

According to Source 2, “the most common emotional response to being ghosted was sadness, reported by 26.21% of participants. Participants also reported low self-esteem after being ghosted, reported by 27.13% of participants.”

This also supports the claim because it shows that ghosting is related with negative emotional reactions and poorer self-evaluation and could be explained by attribution theory. When people are ghosted, they may try to explain why it happened. If they make an internal attribution, they may believe the rejection happened because it is their fault. This can reduce their self-esteem because the person interprets the ghosting as a personal failure rather than as the other person’s behavior.
